title: Novo's next-generation obesity drug shows 25% weight loss in women in late-stage analysis
summary: Novo released new evidence that its experimental CagriSema injection can improve upon the weight loss with its blockbuster GLP-1 obesity injection, Wegovy.
article_text:
In this article
Novo on Tuesday said its next-generation obesity drug, CagriSema, showed 25% weight loss on average among adult women in a new analysis conducted after a late-stage trial.
The Danish company said further work is needed to confirm the hypotheses of two post-study analyses. Still, the results are the latest evidence that the experimental injection can improve upon the weight loss and other benefits offered by Novo's GLP-1 drug semaglutide, the active ingredient in its blockbuster obesity shot Wegovy and diabetes counterpart Ozempic.
CagriSema, a combination of semaglutide and another drug called cagrilintide that targets the amylin pathway, is expected to launch early next year. Obesity drug leaders Novo and Eli Lilly have built new treatments around amylin , which involves a hormone released in the pancreas alongside insulin that helps regulate hunger and fullness, hoping it will give them a new revenue stream beyond existing GLP-1s.
In an analysis of roughly 2,300 women with obesity or who are overweight, CagriSema caused 25% weight loss on average at 68 weeks compared with 3% with placebo. The results are based on an ideal scenario in which all patients stayed on treatment without interruptions.
A second analysis of around 1,900 women assigned by their menopausal status found that weight loss reached 26.7%, 24.8%, and 23.1% in premenopausal, perimenopausal and postmenopausal women, respectively, at 68 weeks, if all patients remained on the drug. That compares with approximately 2% across menopause groups with a placebo.
Across both analyses, CagriSema was linked to reductions in abdominal fat, based on waist circumference, among women overall and across menopause stages, Novo added.
The results suggest that women may experience slightly more weight loss on CagriSema than a broader population of both men and women with obesity saw in the phase 3 trial.
Initial results from the study showed that CagriSema helped adults lose 22.7% of their weight on average at 68 weeks versus 2.3% in the placebo group. However, the majority of patients in the trial — around 67% of roughly 3,400 — were women.
Weight gain is very common for women during menopause. Declining estrogen levels can contribute to a slowdown in metabolism, making it easier for women to gain weight and harder to maintain muscle mass. After menopause, estrogen generally remains low and does not return to previous levels.
More than 86 million women in the U.S. are 40 and older, according to the U.S. Census Bureau , which are the years in which perimenopause, menopause and postmenopause occur.
"Many women with obesity or overweight experience weight gain as they move through menopause, and it is important to explore investigational products such as CagriSema across the reproductive lifespan," said Michelle Skinner Moore, Novo's interim head of clinical development, medical and regulatory affairs.
Wall Street has not appeared particularly excited about CagriSema, whose previous late-stage clinical trial results disappointed investors because the drug showed weight loss efficacy below their expectations. Novo, however, maintains CagriSema is effective and differentiated enough from its other drugs to draw significant demand.
Analysts expect CagriSema to generate $11.84 billion in sales for obesity specifically in 2028, according to a consensus estimate compiled by FactSet.

title: Walmart launches joint membership with Sam's Club as it leans into delivery, gas discounts
summary: Walmart is now offering a joint membership with Sam's Club for $120 per year as the retailer further leans into convenience.
article_text:
In this article
Walmart on Tuesday announced a new joint membership combining its namesake chain and its subsidiary Sam's Club, as the retailer leans further into convenience and value to win over cash-strapped shoppers.
The membership, which combines Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus, will cost $120 per year, according to the company. That price is nearly $100 less than buying individual annual memberships to each retailer, though there is no monthly payment option for the new deal. Both stores will continue to offer standalone options.
"We're giving people a reason to expect more from their memberships," Walmart CEO John Furner said in a statement. "For $120 a year, we're raising expectations for what a membership can deliver: more money in their pockets and more time to call their own."
The membership gives customers access to Sam's Club warehouses, free delivery from both chains, a subscription to Peacock or Paramount+ streaming services, gas savings and 2% Sam's Club cash on eligible purchases. Customers who already have accounts at both stores can link their accounts to receive the discount.
While Walmart's customers often shop for routine, everyday essentials, Sam's Club warehouses offer more opportunity to stock up on bulk purchases. A joint membership could allow the store models to complement one another, according to the company.
The announcement comes as Walmart bets on convenience to drive sales, especially as consumer wallets are squeezed by high gas and food prices.
In August, as Walmart reported fiscal second-quarter earnings, the company raised its outlook for the year, with Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey telling CNBC that consumer spending remained strong despite higher fuel prices. Even so, its stock fell at the time as its sales outlook disappointed Wall Street.
Rainey said in August that the company was lowering prices across various categories, including beef, adding that it's well positioned to weather economic uncertainty because of its emphasis on value and its scale.
Meanwhile, Sam's Club saw a 26% increase in e-commerce sales in the fiscal second quarter, driven by increased transactions and membership growth. The retailer, which also operates its own gas stations, reported net sales of $25.7 billion, including fuel, during that period.
The membership business — which is part of Walmart's push to grow sales with higher profit margins — is already strong. Walmart reported a 17% increase globally in revenue from its membership in the fiscal second quarter with Walmart+ net adds notching a record second-quarter high. For Sam's Club, that revenue number grew 6%.
Walmart added Tuesday that employees at both stores will also receive joint memberships as part of their benefits.
The company said any costs related to the changes in the membership program are not expected to materially impact the company's fiscal third-quarter or full-year guidance.

title: General Motors beats Wall Street's Q3 earnings expectations, narrows full-year guidance
summary: GM narrowed its 2026 earnings guidance and raised its adjusted automotive free cash flow outlook after beating Wall Street’s third-quarter estimates.
article_text:
In this article
DETROIT — General Motors narrowed its 2026 earnings guidance and raised its free cash flow expectations after beating Wall Street's third-quarter expectations.
The Detroit automaker also announced a new multiyear stock buyback of $20 billion after GM completed a $6 billion share repurchase program that was announced in January. GM did not disclose a specific time to complete the program.
Despite the positive news, GM stock was off roughly 6% during premarket trading as the company's outlook missed Wall Street's expectations.
Wall Street analysts were mixed before the report on whether GM would raise its guidance Tuesday amid concerns of slowing sales and rising commodity costs. Analysts' expectations included a midpoint of $13.41 per share for the year compared with GM's new $13.25 per share midpoint, according to LSEG.
Here's how GM performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:
The new guidance includes adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $14.5 billion and $15.5 billion, or $12.75 to $13.75 adjusted earnings per share, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of between $11.5 billion and $12.5 billion.
That compares with its raised guidance from July that included adjusted EBIT of between $14 billion and $16 billion, or $12 to $14 adjusted EPS, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of $9.5 billion to $11.5 billion.
"I think the market's been pretty consistent from what we've said all year," GM CFO Paul Jacobson told CNBC's Phil LeBeau . "Our fourth quarter's going to be down sequentially. ... I think the fact that we're able to hold our guidance in the face of that late inflationary pressure in the year is another sign of the GM team executing really well."
GM on Tuesday said it expects commodity inflation costs to be around $2 billion, which was the high end of its previous guidance. That includes higher costs for logistics and dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, chips that are impacting multiple industries .
While the inflationary costs were at the automaker's high end of guidance, GM said its gross tariff costs are expected to be at the low end of its expected $2.5 billion to $3.5 billion range. Warranty costs are expected to be at high end between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, GM said.
Jacobson said vehicle pricing is relatively flat as inflationary costs continue to increase. He said the company would assess where consumers are in the coming year when deciding if it should pass costs along by raising prices more than normal.
"GM is performing well, and we are working hard to continue our momentum despite growing inflationary pressures through strategic investments in new products and services, and through improved quality and operating efficiency," GM CEO Mary Barra said Tuesday in a letter to shareholders.
The automaker also said the costs of its pullback in all-electric vehicles announced last year were "substantially completed," saying it has recorded $11.2 billion in such charges since the second half of last year, including paying $4.6 billion of $7.4 billion in cash through the third quarter.
The company's net income attributed to stockholders was $3.3 billion during the third quarter, up roughly $2 billion from a year earlier.
GM's North American operations continued to lead the automaker's results, accounting for $3.6 billion of its $4.1 billion in adjusted EBIT results during the third quarter.
GM's 2025 third-quarter results included $48.59 billion in revenue, net income attributable to stockholders of $1.3 billion and earnings per share of $2.80 adjusted.

title: Best Buy launches new gaming hub ahead of 'Zelda' and 'Grand Theft Auto VI'
summary: Best Buy is launching a new gaming experience for customers as it leans into the business ahead of this fall's big launches.
article_text:
In this article
Best Buy is tapping further into a growing customer cohort: gamers.
Chief Revenue Officer Patrick McGinnis told CNBC exclusively that the electronics retailer is launching a new experience Tuesday for customers featuring gaming content, new technology and special offers, among other features. The online destination is called Best Buy Gamers and is launching in a beta version.
"Gamers are a customer that are really like no other in terms of their passion for not just the tech, the titles, but also how they want to work with each other as a community," McGinnis said. "So for us, being relevant for that customer wherever and whenever they want to interact with the thing that they love is really important."
Best Buy says millions of gamers shop at the retailer each year, including trying out games in the store and seeking advice from in-store experts. The new gaming experience, created in partnership with video game website IGN, will offer members gaming articles and reviews, live Best Buy event updates for launches and deals on new technology.
The announcement comes ahead of some of the biggest launches in gaming this year, including the Nov. 5 release of "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time," a remake from Nintendo , and the Nov. 19 launch of Take-Two Interactive 's highly anticipated "Grand Theft Auto VI."
McGinnis said the timing of the rollout is "pretty perfect" given the slate of new video games over the next month, though Best Buy has been developing the new platform for over a year.
"We want to be relevant for our gaming customers, not just during the important, big tentpole periods of the calendar, like when we have these big gaming launches coming up, but really every day," he said. "We want to be there when they discover new titles and connect with the community, and not just when they're buying a big console or a new gaming title."
Best Buy has been leaning into gaming as it sees growing demand from its customers. For its fiscal first-quarter results reported in May, the company said gaming and computing was one of its biggest drivers of growth. On a call with analysts to discuss Best Buy's fiscal second quarter in August, incoming CEO Jason Bonfig said the company expects that demand for "Grand Theft Auto VI" will boost the gaming category.
Best Buy has been looking for growth drivers as the retailer tries to revitalize its business performance under Bonfig. The company has seen slumping sales and was hit by tariffs and lower consumer confidence, among other factors. Tapping into gaming could help revitalize the retailer.
McGinnis said the new gamer experience is an example of the company's strategic goals coming together.
"If you think about what those priorities are, the Gamers [beta] community is definitely a way that we're expanding and growing our reach, reaching that gaming customer," he said. "Providing a place for them to again pursue what they're most passionate about certainly is elevating our experience."
Best Buy is also leaning into in-store experiences around gaming, starting with a location in Torrance, California, next month, where Sony , Nintendo and Microsoft will come together to offer gaming experiences and activations for customers.
With the combination of physical retail and the online platform, McGinnis said, Best Buy hopes to sit at the intersection of technology, entertainment and culture within the gaming community. He said the company plans to tweak its new online experience based on feedback from its customers and continue innovating to meet its audience where it is, especially as the gaming segment continues to be one of the company's strongest performers.
"We recognize the gaming customer as incredibly passionate and wants to engage with what they love in a lot of different ways," he said. "There's observations of gaps that exist in the places and spaces where gamers are engaged, and we thought that we could build something that would really complement what they're engaging with today from a social platform perspective, not to replace those types of experiences in any way, shape or form."

title: Robot factories and hypersonic missiles: JPMorgan Chase's first $5 billion of defense investments
summary: With $5 billion already deployed off its balance sheet, JPMorgan Chase is racing ahead on direct investments in defense tech, hardware and supply chains.
article_text:
In this article
JPMorgan Chase has made $5 billion in startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliency initiative , the company said Monday, a faster-than-expected pace that indicates the bank is finding plentiful opportunities in emerging defense, manufacturing and supply chain firms.
The bank, which last year said it would deploy $10 billion into startups over a decade, may expand the program beyond that initial dollar amount, JPMorgan co-President Doug Petno told CNBC in an interview.
Todd Combs, the former Berkshire Hathaway executive who leads the JPMorgan group in charge of making startup investments , has "hit the ground running," Petno said. "He's done a great job and put us in some really interesting companies," he added.
Most of those investments have yet to be disclosed, but two known stakes seem emblematic of the project's mission to bolster companies that are needed for a more dangerous and chaotic era of geopolitics. JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets, has taken direct stakes in defense-related startups Hadrian and Castelion .
Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as trade disputes with China, have threatened the flow of energy and key components needed for U.S. industries and defense, which spurred JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon into creating the initiative a year ago.
He put Petno, widely seen as one of two key possible successors , in charge of the overall investment project. Combs, a former board member of the bank, reports directly to Dimon.
The scope of the project extends beyond supply chain, defense and manufacturing to include frontier technologies and the pharmaceutical and health-tech industries.
"There's a lot of really interesting companies that have been working to solve some of these problems," Petno said.
These "early venture-stage, advanced manufacturing companies have found ways to build these capabilities in the U.S." rather than relying on overseas trading partners, he said.
In August, the bank helped lead a $1.4 billion funding round for Hadrian, which builds automated factories that make parts for the defense, aerospace and maritime sectors. A California factory run by Hadrian has 10 robots for every human employee, according to the startup's founder.
That month, JPMorgan was also involved in a $1 billion funding round for Castelion, whose flagship product is a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile called Blackbeard. Castelion was founded in late 2022 by a group of former SpaceX engineers.
"Our approach is to find generational companies and partner with them for the long term," Combs said in a statement Monday.
"Putting more than $5 billion to work in our first year shows how many exceptional businesses are building in industries that strengthen critical supply chains," Combs said.
JPMorgan making billions of dollars of direct investments in nascent companies is a departure from its usual role as a lender and advisor.
Before the defense initiative, the bank had moved away from taking startup stakes, which can be relatively risky bets on unproven technologies. JPMorgan spun off its private equity business, One Equity Partners, more than a decade ago.
In its more traditional role, JPMorgan has also financed and facilitated more than $230 billion for industries that support American national interests, according to the bank.
That part of its security and resiliency project, meant to hit $1.5 trillion over 10 years, is led by Jay Horine , a former co-head of investment banking.
JPMorgan built a team for the project of about three dozen bankers, who are aided by hundreds more across the firm, as it expanded the initiative to Europe and Canada.
Its bankers are mapping distribution lines for key products, from submarines and missiles to aircraft, to identify suppliers that may lack the capital or capacity to meet rising demand, according to Petno.
JPMorgan is also in regular communication with the U.S. Department of Defense and Department of Commerce about the government's needs, he said.

title: Here's who Netflix just brought in to run content — and what it means for the streamer
summary: Peter Rice brings a wealth of experience in TV and film, including scripted and unscripted shows, live sports, prestige television and theatrical distribution.
article_text:
In this article
Netflix is shaking up its C-suite in an effort to fix its engagement woes.
On Thursday, the streaming giant announced that former Disney executive Peter Rice will take over as the company's chief content officer, overseeing global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events.
Rice is replacing 10-year Netflix veteran Bela Bajaria , who most recently led the company's global content team with a focus on its live sports strategy . Bajaria was initially hired in 2016 to help the streamer launch an unscripted division as well as licensing and studio co-productions. She later transitioned to the top creative role, spearheading Netflix's $20 billion content budget.
She oversaw popular TV series like "Stranger Things," "Wednesday," "Bridgerton," "Squid Game," "Adolescence" and "Beef," as well as Netflix films like "Frankenstein" and "KPop Demon Hunters." Bajaria also helped push Netflix into live sports and events, including deals with the WWE and the NFL as well as programs like "The Roast of Tom Brady."
Prior to his stint at Disney, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group as well as Fox's lead executive on the Hulu board. He was also the president of Fox Searchlight Pictures and helped release "Slumdog Millionaire," "Juno," "Little Miss Sunshine" and "Sideways."
The executive change follows a tumultuous period for Netflix as it faces stagnating viewership and explores avenues for growth. It comes just days after the streaming giant laid off roughly 1,000 employees , or 6% of its workforce.
The last time Netflix made cuts of this size was in 2022 when it reported its first quarterly subscriber loss in more than 10 years.
"We believe this round of layoffs reflects more structural changes to the cost base than a reaction to near-term subscriber dynamics," wrote Brian Pitz, managing director and head of internet and interactive entertainment equity research at BMO Capital Markets, in a research note published Friday.
In July, Netflix reported viewership increased just 2% in the first half of the year as the streamer suffers from a lack of shows with water-cooler-level hype.
Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted last month during the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company is "not growing as fast as I want us to."
Those warnings, and now Bajaria's exit, have Wall Street bracing for more turbulence ahead.
"The sudden departure of Bajaria likely signals to us that user engagement may have remained soft throughout [the third quarter]," Pitz wrote.
Netflix is set to release fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday.
In July, Nielsen reported that Netflix had generated 7.8% of TV viewership, while YouTube accounted for nearly double that, at 14.2%.
YouTube has been Netflix's biggest threat in the battle for viewers' time. In response, the streaming giant has sought to diversify its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention.
"If the opportunity is to recast [Netflix] into a broader content hub, the risk is missing the watercooler originals," Steven Cahall, equity analyst at Wells Fargo, wrote in a research note last month. "We see breakout hits as a must for the stock to work again."
Rice has a wealth of experience in television and film, most recently serving as the chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the company. He managed a wide swath of channels across broadcast and streaming, including ABC, Disney Channel, Hulu and FX Networks. During his tenure, he oversaw the production of more than 300 shows, including "American Idol," "Modern Family," "Abbott Elementary," "The Bear," "Only Murders in the Building" and "Shogun."
He also headed up major sporting events such as coverage of the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup.
Under Rice's leadership, Disney earned roughly 300 Primetime Emmy nominations between 2021 and 2022. Of those nods, it won nearly 60 awards across its television networks and streaming platforms.
Meanwhile, Netflix's Emmy wins have slowed.
In 2021, it tied the record for most trophies won by an outlet in a single year with 44. This year, however, it only took home 16 prizes, its lowest Emmy haul in a decade.
With Rice, Netflix is also getting an executive with theatrical experience. After he was ousted by then-Disney CEO Bob Chapek in mid-2022, he transitioned into an independent producer role. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later." He's currently developing a movie adaptation of the video game "Elden Ring."
Late last year, Netflix struck a deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery's film studio and streaming assets, only to be outbid months later by Paramount Skydance, which completed its acquisition of WBD in early October.
Some on Wall Street have speculated that the streamer may be interested in further M&A, including acquiring assets from NBCUniversal after it splits from parent company Comcast .
"[Rice's] long tenure at Fox, and then Disney after its acquisition of Fox, gives him unique insight into the consolidation of two major studios, relevant if Netflix chooses to go after another studio," Alicia Reese, senior vice president of equity research at Wedbush, wrote in a research note Thursday. "Even if it doesn't, Rice's experience fits well as Netflix pushes deeper into theatrical and builds a broader platform with varied content across the entertainment ecosystem."

title: Nike's India campus is a long-term growth bet amid turnaround
summary: Nike announced earlier this month that it's expanding into India. The retailer has been broadly struggling, especially in the China market.
article_text:
In this article
Nike is making a big bet on India.
The retailer, which has been struggling to revive its business and regain momentum under CEO Elliott Hill, is hoping the world's most populous country can help it turn the page on its performance.
As it reported its fiscal first-quarter earnings on Oct. 1, the company announced it will create a new global campus in Bengaluru, India, as part of its growth strategy. Hill wrote in a letter to employees that the new facility would be a "long-term investment" to help position Nike for success.
"India is already an important growth market and manufacturing hub for Nike, with strong capabilities and access to talent," Hill wrote.
The new campus is expected to open in the next few years and span corporate roles across the organization, including the namesake Nike brand, Jordan Brand and Converse. Nike plans to discuss its India campus in detail at its investor day next month.
In a statement to CNBC, a Nike spokesperson said expanding into India is a "natural" next step for the company as it looks to grow its global presence.
"As participation in running, basketball, football, fitness and other sports continues to grow across India, we see an opportunity to better serve athletes through stronger local capabilities, consumer insights, and innovation," the spokesperson said.
India will be the world's third-largest retail market by 2030, according to Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries. Its e-commerce market was valued at $159.25 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach $332.94 billion by 2031, according to IBEF, a business advocacy organization created by the Indian government.
Nike has endured a yearslong slump and is trying to right its business under Hill's turnaround plan. Nike also announced this month that it would lay off workers across the company as part of what it has dubbed its Pace strategy, which includes supply chain changes and reorganization of the company's geographic segments. Nike expects the effort to deliver approximately $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031.
Nike's decision to invest further in India as part of its comeback comes as the sportswear company sheds revenue in another critical international market: China. Though its fiscal first-quarter North America revenue came in just above Wall Street expectations, Hill said that performance wasn't enough to offset pressures abroad.
Nike has been particularly struggling in the Greater China market , where its revenue dropped by 26% in its fiscal first quarter. It's part of what experts have said is a broader trend of American companies losing relevance and traction to domestic brands as the once-lucrative market matures.
On a call with analysts earlier this month, Hill said the company was taking "deliberate actions" to strengthen its China business, though he said those effects will take time to materialize. Hill said the company plans to refresh its physical retail, spearhead a digital cleanup and create higher quality experiences for consumers.
The Nike spokesperson told CNBC the company is "deeply committed" to China and sees the region as one of its "most important long-term growth markets," even as Nike expands its presence in India.
"China remains a long-term priority for Nike, while India represents another important opportunity to invest in the future of sport and the next generation of athletes," the spokesperson said.
The company's expansion in India may be coming at both an opportune and inopportune time, according to experts. Investing in a growing international market does not guarantee higher sales — it also requires persuading Indian consumers they want the Nike brand, a challenge the company has struggled to overcome in China.
"What Nike, I think, is doing right now is going region by region and working to reestablish what the brand stands for," Simeon Siegel, a senior managing director at Guggenheim Securities, told CNBC.
Siegel said part of the dissonance for Nike is that each region and segment of the business is at a different stage of its turnaround. He said investing in India may set the company up for a more sustainable future if the China business continues to lag, but Nike needs to have a compelling product, solid storytelling and extensive distribution in the region to be successful there.
"I think the company needs to look inward and figure out what is the right way to reestablish profitability," he said. "And that involves, in certain instances, shrinking and saving and cutting, and, in certain instances, investing and looking toward the future, because the goal here is not to shrink to oblivion; it's to shrink to stability, and then ultimately growth."
The global strategy may also focus too much on a long-term vision rather than more immediate fixes, according to Jessica Ramirez, co-founder and managing director at advisory firm The Consumer Collective, who specializes in retail and apparel. Ramirez said she already thought Nike and Hill's vision were "out of touch" and the plan for the India campus didn't necessarily help its case.
"I don't know that this plan of India is an immediate solution to their problems right now," she said. "They have to plan long term, right? But they also need to plan short term, which is continuously falling apart."
She said Nike has not shared plans that are concrete enough to win back momentum in China and has to develop both regions hand in hand.
While Nike under Hill has improved its wholesale and performance categories, Ramirez said it has yet to master its direct-to-consumer and sportswear segments, which would allow the company to flourish in all of its markets.
The Nike spokesperson told CNBC the retailer is committed to investing in both countries as it tries to expand its global presence.
"Importantly, this is not an either/or decision between India and China," the spokesperson said. "We always invest market by market based on long-term opportunities to serve athletes and grow sport around the world."
Still, India presents an attractive opportunity for many companies looking to unlock growth abroad.
Ramirez said Nike is just the latest to join a cohort of American companies looking to establish their presence in the market. While many brands began investing in China years ago, she said that trend is now pointing toward India instead, as U.S. companies see more spending pressures in the Chinese market and navigate geopolitical tensions between the two countries.
"It's to get in there for the long term and to make sure that they are there for when they can reap the positive effects," she said. "I want to say this conversation started getting a bit more engaging in the last two to three years, when companies started investing more in India."
India is one of the world's strongest market performers, driven primarily by domestic demand, investment and supply-chain diversification, according to an analysis from Accenture. With a population of over 1 billion, the country presents a growth opportunity similar to the one China offered in the early 2000s.
"It's going to be a fast-growing consumer base where we assume their income levels will continue to go up and they'll have much more purchasing power, and so maybe could we be tapping in on that market from a consumer lens," Chris Tomsovic, who leads Accenture's macro foresight team, told CNBC.
Still, one of the biggest focus points for the Indian consumer is price sensitivity, which will pose a challenge for American companies trying to break into the market, he added. Even so, many domestic brands on the market are younger, meaning there could be more opportunities right now for Western companies to take market share.
Another challenge is that the Chinese consumer has historically been receptive to American brands, whereas it will still take more data to understand how Indian shoppers feel about those businesses, he said. For sportswear retailers, the focus of the sports most popular in each region will also factor into that equation.
"Can they really localize the product, make the price point work? Can they adapt to the local social media technology ecosystem? Can they adapt to the local cultural values and norms that the consumer wants?" Tomsovic said.
"If you're able to nail that, then I think you're right. Whether you're a footwear brand, whether you're an athleisure brand, I think there's a huge opportunity there with a billion consumers," he said.

title: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
summary: KFC is switching from PepsiCo to Coca-Cola as its beverage supplier for U.S. restaurants.
article_text:
In this article
KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.
Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast.
The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes.
"This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."
For many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House , its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas.
Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.
KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.
Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.
For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands.
It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway , the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.

title: Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity
summary: Porsche revealed a concept car called Mission S as part of a turnaround plan that includes efforts to boost profits through higher-end products and lower sales.
article_text:
In this article
Porsche on Thursday revealed a concept car called Mission S that signals a new design direction and flagship model for the famed German sports carmaker.
The debut of the sleek midengine vehicle is part of a turnaround plan revealed last week by the Volkswagen -controlled brand that includes efforts to boost profits through higher-end products and lower vehicle sales.
Porsche described Mission S as "a first glimpse of the brand's evolved design identity" that also represents a "super sports car platform" that will be positioned above its iconic 911 sports car.
The vehicle's design is recognizably Porsche but with more aggressive styling compared with its current models, including new hood vents and a roof scoop. Its rear features more differentiated flair in which the vehicle's spoiler flows into its rear panels.
"A Porsche must be recognisable as a Porsche at first glance," Porsche Chairman Michael Leiters said in a release. "The Mission S provides a glimpse of the ideas and design features that will shape Porsche in the coming years."
Automakers routinely use concept vehicles to gauge customer interest, showcase future technologies and signal the direction of a vehicle or brand.
The company did not release expected pricing or performance specifications for such future models. Starting prices for its current 911 models range from roughly $135,500 for an entry-level Carrera to more than $203,000 for a Carrera 4 GTS convertible.
During Porsche's capital markets day on Oct. 7, the company outlined its "Sportwagenschmiede '35" turnaround plan, which focuses on emphasizing high-end sports cars and luxury SUVs to get the carmaker back on track.
Porsche's operating margin last year was only 1.1%, compared with 14.1% in 2024, as the company deals with increased costs, U.S. tariffs and declining sales in China.
The turnaround plan includes a long-term target for a group ‌operating margin of 15% and a midterm breakeven point of 200,000 units or below annually. That compares with sales of 279,449 in 2025.

title: JetBlue’s new domestic first class, BlueFirst, is now on sale
summary: JetBlue announced that BlueFirst, its new domestic first class option, is available for booking on more than 30 routes. It launches December 8.
article_text:
In this article
JetBlue 's new domestic first class , BlueFirst, is now available for booking on flights across more than 30 routes, the airline said Thursday.
This option will be available on domestic flights that are not currently served by the airline's lie-flat Mint business class, which it offers on longer flights. It's part of an overhaul of the carrier's fare options , which will include basic options that don't come with things like seat assignments, a standard option, and a "flex" option, which is refundable and more easily changed.
The new first-class section comes as JetBlue seeks to return to steady profitability by growing its higher-priced offerings amid strong demand for more expensive and roomier seats.
The first flight with BlueFirst seats will be on Dec. 8, between Boston and Fort Lauderdale , Florida, followed by routes between Fort Lauderdale and New York's LaGuardia Airport, with additional flights being rolled out in the following weeks and months.
JetBlue is offering some introductory fares for BlueFirst seats for select flights, including a $299 flight from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, a $249 option from New York to Fort Lauderdale and a $299 option from New York to Liberia, Costa Rica.
The first-class tickets will offer seats that recline up to 5 inches and have up to 7 inches more legroom than Main seats, JetBlue said. Other perks include Bluetooth-connected seatback screens, food and beverage options, Group 1 boarding and expedited security.
Within the BlueFirst class, there are three tiered fare option s:
"We designed BlueFirst to deliver a more accessible first-class experience that combines the thoughtful hospitality and service customers expect from JetBlue with exceptional value and comfort. We're excited that customers can now start making BlueFirst part of their travel plans," JetBlue CEO Joanna Geraghty said in a news release.

title: Southwest is overhauling its frequent flyer program. Here's what's changing
summary: Southwest Airlines is overhauling its loyalty program and replacing A-List and A-List Preferred with three new tiers.
article_text:
In this article
Goodbye, A-List and A-List Preferred.
Southwest Airlines is scrapping its two-tier loyalty program starting next year and instead rolling out silver, gold and platinum levels that are similar to what other carriers offer, as the once-quirky airline seeks to increase revenue and reward its biggest spenders.
Southwest executives have been overhauling the airline, getting rid of longtime customer perks like two free checked bags and open seating . It's now charging for some of those options, like rivals have been doing for years.
Along with the shift from two to three loyalty levels, the carrier is also changing the names of its tiers. Under the old version, travelers could be classified into A-List or A-List Preferred, which was the higher level.
"If you think about A-List and A-List Preferred, we don't even have [boarding] groups A, B and C anymore," Tony Roach, Southwest chief customer and brand officer, said in an interview. "So it was time to do a refresh to somewhat incorporate all the changes to seating and all these new experiences that we've been adding."
Here's what's changing for the loyalty program:
Customers can earn 1 Tier Qualifying Point, or TQP, per $1 spent on Southwest co-branded credit cards with Chase . Here are the new status requirements:
Silver status members will board in Group 1, while Gold members will board before Group 1. Platinum members will board before both Gold members and Group 1. Platinum tier also has unlimited Companion Pass trips.
Southwest's Companion Pass — which lets a designated person fly for free, minus taxes and fees, with a traveler who has that perk — is also changing.
Companion Pass holders that have them in their accounts will be able to hold onto them for the duration of their term. But starting with the 2027 earning year, Companion Pass benefits will be earned through TQPs or qualifying flights, by hitting a milestone reward or with Platinum status.
Currently, a Rapid Rewards member has to earn at least 135,000 qualifying points or 100 one-way flights to qualify for the pass.
The airline is also expanding its partnerships with international airlines and building its first airport lounges. Southwest on Thursday offered a peek into the new lounges , which it has named Icon, and is working on with its credit card partner, Chase . The carrier is building Icon lounges in four cities around the U.S., with others in the works.
Southwest is also adding benefits for customers that are in between status tiers, similar to what American Airlines offers.
For example, after earning 20,000 points or taking 15 qualifying flights, customers can choose between 2,000 more Rapid Rewards points or two coupons to select a "preferred" seat, which is a standard legroom seat that's closer to the front of the plane or a more popular aisle or window seat.
Customers will also get three Companion Pass trips after earning 95,000 points or taking 75 qualifying flights, which is below the Platinum threshold.
"That is definitely different from what we've done before," said Nandika Suri, who heads Southwest's Rapid Rewards loyalty program. She said the new strategy is "a way for us to actually recognize and reward customers ... faster and more frequently in their journey to continue to engage with us."
Airlines overall have consistently raised the requirements to earn status, requiring more spending, and have made similar changes to enter their airport lounges.
United Airlines on Tuesday said it would no longer allow customers to earn status in its Mileage Plus program based on flight segments next year and that it would only accept Premier qualifying points, which are earned from flight spending and on a co-branded credit card.
United also raised the requirements to reach Premier 1K, its highest frequent flyer tier outside of the invite-only Global Services, to 32,000 qualifying points, up from 28,000 this year.
— CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this article.

title: How lower fuel economy targets could boost pickups and V-8 engines
summary: An analyst who follows the industry says there are four ways recent changes to fuel economy rules will shift investment toward the most profitable segments.
article_text:
Automakers could see a financial tail wind that runs in the billions of dollars after the U.S. lowered fuel economy standards and stopped issuing fines for violations of those rules, according to an auto analyst.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration in late September sharply reduced fuel economy targets for light-duty vehicles to an average of 34.9 miles per gallon by 2031. Under the previous rules the Biden administration finalized in 2024, the U.S. fleet was then expected to average 50.4 miles per gallon by the same time.
That followed Congress voting last year to eliminate the fines automakers faced for failing to comply with regulations. Several years ago, General Motors and Stellantis paid hundreds of millions of dollars in civil penalties for failing to meet U.S. fuel economy requirements for prior model years, Reuters reported.
"We've already seen [costs from fines and credits] come down even this year and serve as incremental earnings tail winds," said Itay Michaeli, an analyst for TD Cowen. "And it could be a few to several hundred million dollars."
The new rules also eliminate the selling and trading of credits automakers use to compensate for producing fuel-thirsty vehicles. The NHTSA has in the past allowed automakers at risk of exceeding their fuel economy average to buy credits from others that make low- or zero-emission vehicles.
Historically, state and federal credits have been revenue sources for electric vehicle producers such as Tesla and Rivian .
Those changes take the pressure off automakers that have tended to produce less-efficient vehicles — such as SUVs, pickup trucks or high-performance sports cars. But they also allow automakers to redirect their portfolios and investments away from products made for compliance and toward ones that are more profitable, Michaeli said.
There are three pieces to the potential strategy shift, he said. First, automakers can sell more internal-combustion vehicles and fewer of what are often called "compliance cars," which are slower-selling or less profitable fuel-efficient vehicles or EVs that automakers make in order to stay on the right side of fuel economy or emissions rules.
In the past year, several automakers have written down billions in EV-related investments, showing how those vehicles have been difficult to make profitable in the U.S.
Ford announced a $19.5 billion special charge in December as part of a business restructuring and a pullback in EV investments, while GM recorded a $7.1 billion impact in the fourth quarter related to its own pullback and restructuring in China. At Porsche, EV-related write-downs drove automotive operating profit down 98% in 2025, and Honda's contributed to the company's first annual loss in about 70 years.
A second possible change is what Michaeli calls "ICE optimization" — the loosened regulations allow automakers to sell more high-margin vehicles, which often come with larger engines.
Detroit automakers, and some foreign ones, have already been reintroducing V-8 engines. Stellantis' Ram brand has brought the gas-guzzling engines back for its full-size pickup line. GM, meanwhile, said in September that it will bring a new generation of small-block V-8 engines to its full-size Silverado and Sierra pickup trucks. And Ford has increased V-8 availability across its F-150 pickups, the top-selling vehicle in the U.S.
"So to kind of work down the funnel," Michaeli said automakers might be thinking, "I don't have to pay compliance costs, I don't have to buy credits. That's great. Now I can maybe sell more pickup trucks, and within those pickup trucks, I could sell more V-8s and different trims of those pickup trucks."
Michaeli said the third piece is that automakers are also redirecting research and development investments away from projects focused on meeting fuel-efficiency regulations and toward those that either boost profits or support further investment in powertrain development or other technology.
After both the elimination of federal tax credits for EVs and the market pullback in that segment, automakers are left with big questions about how to invest, said John Murphy, an automotive analyst.
"Balance sheets and cash on balance sheet may need to be far higher than they thought previously, because there's such extreme uncertainty around where powertrains need to ultimately go," Murphy said. "Remember, powertrain is the most expensive part of a vehicle."
Despite regulatory changes, hybrids have surged in the U.S. market over the past several months, and some companies have been better positioned for that increase than others. Murphy expects that to continue.
"Our forecasts are that hybrids, absent a change in the regulatory regime, will go from 14% of the market last year to about 34% of the market by the end of the decade," he said. "So that's a big shift that's happening quickly. There are some months where we've been about 19% [hybrids]."
That said, Michaeli argued that EVs are still likely to continue growth. Electric vehicles have an exceptionally high loyalty rate, he said.
EV owners are more likely to replace their vehicle with another EV than hybrid or gasoline-vehicle owners are to stay with the same powertrain type, Michaeli said. EVs are also still preferred platforms for other innovative technologies, such as autonomous driving features.
But the main reason Michaeli sees potential for EVs is the sheer number of two-car households in the U.S. — the highest share of such households in the world. Michaeli said he thinks those households are most likely to opt for one EV and one ICE vehicle. There are roughly 300 million vehicles on U.S. roads today, he said. Only about 7.5 million of those are EVs, according to the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a trade group for automakers.
"A lot of next-generation EVs are still coming," he said. "Imagine what happens as those EVs hit the market and ramp. That's why it's really hard to be negative structurally on U.S. EV demand, because when it turns, it can turn very, very sharply."

title: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos
summary: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic’s Mythos, offering a rare look at costs involved in defending against AI.
article_text:
In this article
Bank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligence models including Anthropic's Mythos , the bank's CEO, Brian Moynihan , told CNBC on Wednesday.
In an interview after the bank's third-quarter earnings release , Moynihan said that earlier this year the company rushed to bolster a wide spectrum of its internal and vendor code using thousands of employees and outside personnel.
"That risk is real risk, and that's why when the frontier-type models came out. … A lot of us sat down and said, 'How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?" Moynihan told CNBC's Leslie Picker .
"We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area," he said.
The bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" on the software remediation and regulatory issues related to anti-money laundering compliance in the third quarter, Moynihan told analysts earlier Wednesday.
The comments are some of the first by a major U.S. corporation to specify the manpower and dollars spent to protect software systems from Mythos, which was released to a small group of banks, technology firms and government agencies in April.
They also highlight the dual-edged nature of AI: While it can help companies save money by boosting productivity, the ability of models like Mythos to uncover and exploit decades-old software flaws has also forced firms into a costly defensive scramble.
"We've got to stay ahead of them, and we've got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services," Moynihan said.
Still, Moynihan — speaking as his company's shares slumped as much as 8% Wednesday — sought to reassure investors that the spending increase was temporary.
"Once you patch, you don't have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through," Moynihan said, adding that the bank expects remediation costs to decline over time.
In other places, AI is helping to reduce expenses. Bank of America has about 130 internal AI projects, and savings from those efforts are expected to rise from $300 million this year to $700 million in 2027, Moynihan told analysts.
Bank of America's head count fell by about 3,400 employees in the past year as the firm cut roughly 5% of managers, he said. It's unclear how much of that workforce reduction is attributable to AI.

title: Merck CEO tells CNBC he expects breakthrough cancer vaccine will become faster to make
summary: His comments come after Merck officially opened its new 120,000-square-foot research facility in the Greater Philadelphia area.
article_text:
In this article
Merck CEO Rob Davis told CNBC on Wednesday that he expects the company's breakthrough cancer vaccine with Moderna to get faster to manufacture over time.
Shortening the current six-week timeline could potentially help the companies reach more patients.
"We are going to drive for improvement, but right now the focus really is, let's make sure we have the supply ready, we have the market ready to bring this important innovation to the market, and then we'll talk about how do we accelerate," he told CNBC in an exclusive interview. "But I do think over time you're going to see that timeline shortened."
The personalized cancer vaccine turnaround spans from sequencing a patient's tumor to delivering it to the hospital. Merck and Moderna's vaccine is designed to target the specific mutations in each individual patient's tumor rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach, which makes it complicated to produce.
The idea is to train the immune system to recognize and kill those unique cancer markers and then pair that response with Merck's blockbuster immunotherapy Keytruda, which aims to help the body attack the cancer more effectively.
Davis acknowledged that manufacturing the vaccine is a "complex system," but said Merck and Moderna have the process "down to a very tight science."
"I'm actually very confident that we're not going to have complexities in getting this to patients in a very timely fashion," he added. "We're doing it in our clinicals, and I only see improvement going forward."
His comments come after the two companies in August released positive initial data from a late-stage trial on the shot in combination with Keytruda in melanoma patients. Davis said the company is also examining the vaccine in trials across other tumors, including non-small cell lung cancer, types of bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma.
"You like to talk that maybe you can start moving toward talking about a cure," he said. "We're not there yet, but we're moving in a direction with technology that's really unprecedented."
Davis spoke to CNBC after Merck earlier Wednesday officially opened its new 120,000-square-foot research facility , which it has named Advance, in its West Point, Pennsylvania, campus. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro joined Merck executives and other government officials for a ribbon-cutting ceremony to celebrate the launch of the facility, which features highly automated robotic systems and advanced digital AI capabilities.
Merck says the facility is designed to streamline the analysis of biological samples from the company's ongoing drug programs and improve its research and development.
The opening of the new facility comes as Merck prepares for the upcoming loss of exclusivity of Keytruda, which is one of the world's top-selling drugs and is widely viewed as the backbone of modern cancer treatment. Keytruda's core U.S. compound patent expires in December 2028, while secondary patents extend protection into 2029 and beyond.
Merck has implemented a multi-layered strategy to turn the Keytruda transition into what it views as a manageable "hill" rather than a sharp revenue cliff. That includes accelerating internal research and also funneling $65 billion in external acquisitions and licensing agreements over the five years to build its pipeline of next-generation medicines.
The pharmaceutical giant is also developing new forms of Keytruda and combination regimens that it can transition patients onto and protect the drug's revenue even after key patents expire before 2030.
The Food and Drug Administration in September 2025 approved the subcutaneous form of Keytruda, which is considered a more convenient version because it is administered under the skin in minutes. The standard form of the drug is an intravenous infusion that takes around 30 minutes.
But Merck is facing a legal battle over the newer version in some European markets, raising questions about the market size for the drug.
A Dutch court issued an injunction earlier this month blocking Merck from selling, stocking or manufacturing subcutaneous Keytruda across eight European countries: Belgium, Denmark, France, Ireland, Italy, Sweden, Switzerland and the Netherlands. That followed a patent infringement suit brought by the biotech company Halozyme Therapeutics over its own subcutaneous drug delivery platform.
Merck has said it strongly disagrees with the rulings and plans to appeal. Patients can still receive the original form of Keytruda in Europe while the patent dispute unfolds.
Still, Halozyme has also sued Merck for patent infringement ​in ⁠the U.S., alleging the subcutaneous formulation of Keytruda infringes 15 patents that the biotech has filed since 2011.
Meanwhile, Merck is focused on rolling out a slate of new drugs. That includes Winrevair, a treatment for a rare, life-threatening lung disease that was approved in 2024 and acquired a few years earlier through its $11.5 billion acquisition of Acceleron .
Another closely watched launch is Merck's cholesterol-lowering pill Lipfendra, which was approved by the FDA in July.

title: Netflix to lay off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of workforce
summary: Netflix will lay off roughly 6% of its workforce, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.
article_text:
In this article
Netflix said on Wednesday it will lay off roughly 6% of its employees, or roughly 1,000 workers, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.
The job cuts will largely impact the product, tech, legal and HR teams.
"Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources," Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in the email to employees. "Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full year forecast. We'll continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation.
"Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors," the note said.
Netflix said it did not have additional comments beyond the co-CEOs' memo. The company is due to report quarterly earnings on Oct. 20.
The layoffs come just a few weeks after Sarandos told attendees at the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company was "not growing as fast as I want."
Netflix has faced a paradox in recent months. It continues to post solid profits and remains the biggest player in the streaming realm, but its viewing time has stagnated and the main driver of new subscriber acquisitions has been its password-sharing crackdown and the launch of a cheaper, ad-supported tier.
Netflix's biggest threat has been YouTube, but looming on the horizon is Skydance . The combined entity of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery has plans to integrate the two companies' streaming platforms, Paramount+ and HBO Max.
Netflix has diversified its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention. At the same time, it's lacked the water-cooler-type hits like "Stranger Things" and "Squid Game" that previously boosted subscriber growth and viewership.
And Netflix is not the only company looking to cut costs in the media space. Last month, Disney said it would lay off around 300 employees , with the majority of cuts coming from human resources and technology roles.
— CNBC's Julia Boorstin and Stephen Desaulniers contributed to this report.

title: Morgan Stanley tops estimates as equities trading revenue beats expectations by $909 million
summary: Morgan Stanley topped expectations on the top and bottom lines for the third quarter.
article_text:
In this article
Morgan Stanley posted third-quarter results that beat expectations on blockbuster results in its equities trading franchise.
Here's what the company reported:
The company said profit climbed 6.5% to $4.91 billion, or $3.03 a share. Revenue rose 12% to $20.34 billion.
The firm's equities trading division, long a marquee business for Morgan Stanley, posted a 41% increase in revenue to $5.8 billion, exceeding the StreetAccount estimate by about $909 million.
Morgan Stanley noted widespread strength across its equities products and regions, but cited Asia as a source of particular strength in the quarter. The gains in that business helped offset disappointments elsewhere.
Fixed income trading revenue fell 7% to $2.01 billion, driven by declines in credit and commodities, which is roughly $260 million below expectations.
Investment banking revenue edged 2% higher to $2.16 billion, about $110 million below expectations. The bank cited an increase in advisory revenue on more completed mergers, but declines in equity underwriting on lower initial public offerings and a drop in fixed income underwriting.
Still, the results were "good, but not great," as some business metrics showed slower improvement in the quarter, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo said Wednesday in a note.
Morgan Stanley shares declined about 3% Wednesday.
The economy is subject to two key forces right now: the boost from the artificial intelligence build-out and the drag from geopolitical strife, Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick told CNBC's Leslie Picker on Wednesday.
Starting in early September, concerns with overseas conflict, inflation and surging yields slowed activity across Wall Street, Pick noted.
"The interaction of the AI phenomenon and geopolitics has been the dominant reality the whole year," Pick said. "It's really two very different stories, and I'd like to think that we are going to have the first narrative, the positive narrative, if we can get some control over the geopolitics."
Pick is "cautiously optimistic" about markets in the fourth quarter, he added.

title: Delta's business-class revamp: New seats, menus, plates and more Porsches
summary: Delta is upgrading its top-tier Delta One cabin with new suites for its largest A350 plane, starting next year.
article_text:
In this article
Delta Air Lines , the country's most profitable airline, has a problem serving its top-tier customers: not enough Porsches.
The airline uses a fleet of 40 of the luxury vehicles to drive its high-value flyers right to the plane.
"What's happened over the last several years is the demand has continued to rise, and we realized that the 40 cars that we have weren't enough to meet the demand. So we're moving that fleet to 70," Ranjan Goswami, Delta's chief marketing and product officer, told CNBC.
It's just one of many changes Delta is making for customers who fly in its most luxurious and expensive cabin, known as Delta One . The Porsche service is part of a VIP add-on option.
The carrier on Wednesday unveiled new crockery for the cabins, new Missoni mini pillows and fresh food and beverage menus, including Champagne served over sorbet and Blanton's bourbon. Many of the new items will appear on flights originating in Los Angeles later this month and on other routes in the coming months.
Delta is also planning to debut updated suites with a bigger screen and a more cushioned, lighter lie-flat seat when it starts flying its first Airbus A350-1000 planes early next year.
Delta didn't announce changes to the coach and premium economy cabins.
The airline's executives said the company is already thinking about adjustments on other aircraft, including smaller Airbus jets and on Boeing 787 Dreamliners that Delta has ordered and that will come in the next decade.
Delta has invested heavily in premium service for close to two decades, and United Airlines has followed suit for a little over 10 years. Other carriers are also leaning into demand for higher-priced options.
"You got to keep looking at the next cycle of what customers want, and you got to start planning for it now," Goswami said.
He said Delta focused on details and quality with its latest project for Delta One so that the items, from sliding suite doors to new Delta-logo-emblazoned dinnerware, are made to last. The company tested some of those items to check for chipping, but there are other challenges, like customers liking them too much.
"I think people are going to love a couple of items, although we hope they don't steal them," he said.

title: Bank of America shares drop after third-quarter revenue miss and regulatory penalty
summary: Bank of America shares fell Wednesday after the company posted weaker-than-expected trading revenue and the impact of a $1.2 billion Treasury fine.
article_text:
In this article
Bank of America on Wednesday posted a sharp profit decline after being hit with a $1.2 billion penalty by U.S. regulators, while revenue also disappointed after trading operations generated about $750 million less than expected.
Shares of the bank fell almost 5% on Wednesday.
Here's what the company reported:
The bank's third-quarter profit fell 17% to $6.93 billion, or 91 cents a share. Excluding the penalty, which sapped income by 17 cents, EPS would've been $1.08 a share.
Companywide revenue rose 3.2% to $30.12 billion in the quarter, on an FTE basis, but that was below expectations by about $570 million, largely on misses from Wall Street trading operations.
Fixed income trading revenue dropped 17% to $2.55 billion on weakness in mortgages, municipals and credit activity. That is roughly $450 million below the StreetAccount estimate.
Equities trading revenue climbed 10% to $2.51 billion, but that was also below analysts' expectations, by nearly $300 million.
The trading disappointment comes after CEO Brian Moynihan told analysts last month that trading revenue would be roughly flat; instead the combined bond and stock trading results fell by 5%.
Investment banking revenue dropped 11% to $1.8 billion, roughly in line with expectations and Moynihan's September guidance.
Net interest income, a key profitability driver watched closely by Bank of America investors, rose 7.9% to $16.6 billion, slightly edging out the $16.53 billion StreetAccount estimate.
In a research note published Wednesday, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo called the firm's capital markets results "easily worst in class" for the quarter.
The Treasury episode, in which U.S. regulators said the company failed to report billions of dollars in suspicious transactions, sparked questions as to whether Moynihan has a handle on controls at the second-biggest U.S. bank by assets.
On the company's earnings call Wednesday, several analysts remarked on the sharp decline in Bank of America shares and pressed Moynihan about earlier guidance that compliance costs would be contained.
"Clearly you've had a huge charge this morning," JPMorgan analyst Vivek Juneja said. "It's not that you can't absorb a billion. … But obviously it's a reputational and confidence issue."
Other analysts questioned management on the pace of future share repurchases and asked about the bank's underperformance in trading. Management blamed the firm's bond trading results on the sharp rise in interest rates during the period.
"It just happens when rates go up 85 basis points in a quarter, that tends not to be good for" credit and mortgage trading businesses, CFO Alastair Borthwick said.
Later Wednesday in an interview with CNBC's Leslie Picker , Moynihan didn't commit to a timeline on the resolution of regulatory issues.
"We got to do the work, and then the regulators look at it," Moynihan said. "So I don't want to speculate about the precise timeline."
The CEO added that he was "confident that we are on the right course to remediate everything."
Moynihan took the helm in 2010 and spent the early years of his tenure making amends for mortgage-related abuses in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis.
The Treasury fine, announced on Tuesday, added 11th-hour intrigue to what was an otherwise fairly routine bank earnings week. On Tuesday, JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo posted mixed results, with JPMorgan missing EPS and revenue estimates for the first time in years.
Correction: Bank of America reported third-quarter revenue on an FTE basis of $30.12 billion compared with LSEG estimates of $30.69 billion. An earlier version misstated the comparison.

title: United Airlines is making it harder to reach its top frequent flyer status in 2027
summary: United Airlines is doing away with flight segment as a way to reach Premier status and increasing the spending requirements for Premier 1K.
article_text:
In this article
United Airlines is getting rid of one path to achieve elite status in 2027 and making its top tier harder to reach.
The Chicago-based airline is removing the ability for MileagePlus members to earn status partially based on flight segments flown in a calendar year for 2027. Instead, starting Jan. 1, United will only consider the number of points members earn based on Premier qualifying points earned from eligible flight spending, award travel and eligible United credit card spending.
United announced the change Tuesday in emails to MileagePlus members and on its website . The change aims to simplify how customers earn Premier status, according to the email obtained by CNBC that United sent to members.
Previously, members could gain status in the lowest elite tier, Premier Silver, with a combination of 15 flight segments and 5,000 points earned in a year, or with 6,000 points. Now, customers will only be able to achieve the status through points at the 6,000 point threshold.
The number of Premier qualifying points it will take for members to reach the Premier Gold and Platinum tiers through points will also stay the same as the previous points-only option. However, to reach United's highest rewards tier, Premier 1K, members now need 32,000 qualifying points, up from 28,000 in 2026.
Flyers earn one Premier qualifying point, or PQP, per dollar spent on United base fares and upgrades, and for every 100 miles they redeem for travel on United flights. United Chase cardholders also earn points when they spend money with their card.
MileagePlus members will still have to take at least four flights on United or United Express jets in a year to be eligible for Premier status.
In an interview with travel website The Points Guy , United's President of MileagePlus Jarad Fisher called the flight segments metric an "old relic," saying that the airline "thought it made more sense for them to have one consistent metric ... that they could focus on across the board between their flight activity, their engagement in the airline."
United also announced Tuesday that United cardholders who have Premier status will get a head start by automatically receiving 5% of the points needed to reach the status level they earned the previous year when a new year begins.
United earlier this year overhauled the way travelers earn miles to reward customers holding its credit cards. The carrier also slashed earnings for basic economy flights, following earlier changes to the same practice by American Airlines and Delta Air Lines . United previously upped the thresholds required to earn Premier status in 2024 for the 2025 qualification year.

title: Airport attacks put aviation in crosshairs of geopolitical conflicts
summary: Deadly attacks at Riyadh’s main airport are disrupting airlines, closing airspace and raising new security questions for commercial aviation.
article_text:
In this article
Deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport over the past week are highlighting how conflicts in the Middle East are upending air travel on a larger scale.
Aviation is increasingly in the middle of these sprawling clashes as threats and outright attacks have forced airlines to quickly cancel flights throughout the Middle East for days, weeks and, in some cases, months. Some carriers might redeploy planes that would be going to some Middle East destinations like Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and Doha, Qatar, to other locations altogether.
"It's a new paradigm. Civil aviation is being directly targeted and it has not been the case in the last couple of decades," said Mark Zee, founder of OpsGroup, an independent aviation safety group whose members include pilots, dispatchers, airline employees and others.
The Saudi airport attacks , claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, were the deadliest in the country in more than a decade. Over the weekend, at least 13 people were killed and more than 300 injured when a projectile hit terminals at King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, officials said. Other attacks have included drones.
"Historically, airport security is focused on preventing unauthorized access to aircraft and the airport, not defending airspace," said Jeff Price, a professor at the Metropolitan State University of Denver's Department of Aviation and Aerospace Science and an airport management consultant.
The threats to aviation are forcing officials to rethink how to protect blind spots in these major public spaces.
"There is this established way to deal with kind of more conventional weapons such as missiles. It's very expensive, but there is a way," said Gulnaz Ukassova, UAE-based security director of information and analysis at risk management firm International SOS. "There is still no sort of foolproof way to deal with the threat posed by drones. The technology, obviously, is constantly evolving."
King Khalid International Airport has been shut down for much of this week, and some carriers suspended operations there, citing safety concerns. CEOs of major oil companies also pulled out of an energy conference in the country.
Delta Air Lines , meanwhile, was less than two weeks away from launching an Atlanta-Riyadh route , the first nonstop commercial flight between the the two countries operated by a U.S. airline, according to the carrier.
But late Sunday, the Federal Aviation Administration warned U.S. carriers about safety-of-flight risks when flying in or over Saudi Arabia. On Monday morning, Delta said it would postpone the route's debut until March.
The new Delta route comes as Saudi leadership seeks to boost tourism to the country, part of the kingdom's Vision 2030 plan to diversify the economy from oil and attract international investment.
Air traffic in Saudi Arabia had been increasing rapidly. Scheduled growth in airplane seats in the market is up more than 23% this year from 2023, though the rise has recently slowed, according to aviation-data firm Cirium.
Whether travelers come back to the region depends on risk appetite. Ukassova said energy companies, which can depend on in-person visits to large projects, tend to have higher risk tolerance, while academics have a low bar for potential risks.
The conflicts have cut off big parts of airspace in the Middle East, mainly over Iran . The outbreak of the Iran war in February set off massive aviation, travel and safety crises.
For example, Australian carrier Qantas has changed its Perth, Australia-to-London route to avoid Iranian airspace. Because that flight is then longer, the carrier has added a stop in Singapore to refuel.
For four years, Western commercial passenger and cargo planes have already had to fly longer routes to avoid Russian airspace . Carriers started detouring away from Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Taking longer routes to avoid potentially dangerous airspace has been adding to airlines' fuel bills , which got even more expensive this year due to those same Middle East conflicts.
While much of the traffic to Dubai and Doha has rebounded from the first days of the war since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, it remains below 2025 levels, according to flight-data firm OAG. Capacity by seats across the Middle East is down 5.7% in October from last year, 2.2 million fewer seats, OAG reported.
Some airlines are opting to stay away from the region altogether.
"We will not fly to Dubai and Doha, and we need to wait until the situation gets settled," Finnair CEO Turkka Kuusisto told reporters last month in New York.

title: Walmart to cover some GLP-1s, inhalers and insulin for employees at no cost as it expands benefits
summary: Walmart will offer Novo's Ozempic and Lilly's Mounjaro without charge for people with Type 2 diabetes after a new prior authorization.
article_text:
In this article
Walmart plans to cover more than 250 prescriptions, including some insulin, inhalers and GLP-1s for diabetes, at no cost to its employees in 2027, the company confirmed to CNBC on Tuesday.
The retailer is also expanding existing benefits and adding new ones to attract and retain workers at a time when many other employers are offsetting rising healthcare costs with higher prices and scaled-back plan benefits. The announcement comes weeks before open enrollment for Walmart employees closes on Nov. 6.
Walmart, the biggest private employer in the U.S., will offer Novo's diabetes injection Ozempic and Eli Lilly's rival shot Mounjaro without charge for people with Type 2 diabetes after a new prior authorization.
But the company still does not cover GLP-1s from Novo and Lilly for the purpose of weight loss. Other large employers similarly don't cover those treatments for obesity or have recently dropped coverage to tamp down on their healthcare costs.
